The graph above shows the velocity of an object moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis. At time $t=2$ the particle is located at the position $x=-1.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=8?$
examples.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t = 8$ is equal to its position at $t=2$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [2,8].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(8) = x(2)+ \int_2^8 v(t) \, \textrm d t
$$

We are told that $x(2)=-1$, and we can compute the integral $\displaystyle\int_2^8 v(t) \, \textrm dt$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=2$ to $t=8.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
\int_2^8 v(t) \, \textrm dt = 6.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(8) = -1+ 6 = 5
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=8$ is $x=5.$

feedback.problem:
A particle $Q$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)\operatorname{tan}⁡(t).$ At time $t=0$ the particle is located at the position $x=3.$ 
Find the position of the particle at time $t=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Do not round the answer.

The position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ is $x=$
{{field-1}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{3}].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\frac{\pi }{3})=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =3+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =3+{[\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)]}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =3+\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0) \\  & =3+2-1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ is $x=4.$
